claim: Billions of apoptotic cells are removed daily in a human adult by professional phagocytes (e.g. macrophages) and neighboring nonprofessional phagocytes (e.g. stromal cells).
source: Billions of apoptotic cells are removed daily in a human adult by professional phagocytes (e.g. macrophages) and neighboring nonprofessional phagocytes (e.g. stromal cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about apoptotic cell clearance mechanisms and is presented as background information.

claim: Neutrophils are thought to be excluded from apoptotic sites to avoid tissue inflammation.
source: Despite being a type of professional phagocyte, neutrophils are thought to be excluded from apoptotic sites to avoid tissue inflammation.
evidence: This represents the prevailing scientific view prior to the current study, supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: Neutrophils are the predominant phagocyte responsible for the clearance of apoptotic hepatic cells in the steady state.
source: Here, we report a fundamental and unexpected role of neutrophils as the predominant phagocyte responsible for the clearance of apoptotic hepatic cells in the steady state.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations in human and mouse liver samples shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Neutrophils burrow directly into apoptotic hepatocytes in a process termed perforocytosis.
source: In contrast to the engulfment of dead cells by macrophages, neutrophils burrowed directly into apoptotic hepatocytes, a process we term perforocytosis
evidence: This mechanism is demonstrated through microscopy images and videos showing neutrophils penetrating apoptotic hepatocytes.

claim: Neutrophils ingest apoptotic hepatocytes from the inside.
source: neutrophils burrowed directly into apoptotic hepatocytes, a process we term perforocytosis, and ingested the effete cells from the inside.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy and electron microscopy images showing neutrophils inside apoptotic hepatocytes.

claim: Depletion of neutrophils causes defective removal of apoptotic bodies in mouse liver.
source: The depletion of neutrophils caused defective removal of apoptotic bodies, induced tissue injury in the mouse liver
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing increased apoptotic hepatocytes in neutrophil-depleted mice (Figure 5D).

claim: Neutrophil depletion induces tissue injury in the mouse liver.
source: The depletion of neutrophils caused defective removal of apoptotic bodies, induced tissue injury in the mouse liver
evidence: Supported by liver function analysis showing increased AST, ALT, and bilirubin levels in neutrophil-depleted mice (Figure 6A-D).

claim: Neutrophil depletion leads to the generation of autoantibodies.
source: The depletion of neutrophils caused defective removal of apoptotic bodies, induced tissue injury in the mouse liver, and led to the generation of autoantibodies.
evidence: Demonstrated by detection of increased autoantibodies (anti-SMA, anti-ANA, anti-LKM, total IgG) in neutrophil-depleted mice (Figure 6E-H).

claim: Human autoimmune liver disease shows defects in neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic hepatic cells.
source: Human autoimmune liver disease showed similar defects in the neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic hepatic cells.
evidence: Supported by analysis of AIL patient samples showing apoptotic hepatocytes not phagocytosed by neutrophils (Figure 7A) and decreased phagocytosis ability of AIL neutrophils (Figure 7B).

claim: Neutrophils possess a specialized immunologically silent mechanism for the clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes through perforocytosis.
source: Hence, neutrophils possess a specialized immunologically silent mechanism for the clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes through perforocytosis
evidence: Inferred from observations that neutrophil influx into apoptotic hepatocytes does not cause detectable tissue injury or inflammation.

claim: Defects in neutrophil-mediated apoptotic clearance contribute to the genesis of autoimmune liver disease.
source: defects in this key housekeeping function of neutrophils contribute to the genesis of autoimmune liver disease.
evidence: Supported by data showing neutrophil depletion leads to autoantibody generation and AIL patients have defective neutrophil phagocytosis.

claim: An estimated hundred billion cells undergo apoptosis daily in a human adult.
source: An estimated hundred billion cells undergo apoptosis daily in a human adult (Fond and Ravichandran, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Apoptotic cells must be disposed of promptly and efficiently without littering cytoplasm or causing inflammation.
source: These apoptotic cells must be disposed of promptly and efficiently without littering cytoplasm or causing inflammation (Franz et al., 2006).
evidence: This represents established scientific understanding supported by citation.

claim: Defects in the clearance of apoptotic bodies are often linked to various inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.
source: Defects in the clearance of apoptotic bodies are often linked to various inflammatory and autoimmune diseases (Nagata et al., 2010; Poon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Apoptotic bodies are believed to be cleared by professional phagocytes such as macrophages and immature dendritic cells, or by local nonprofessional phagocytes.
source: It is widely believed that apoptotic bodies are cleared by professional phagocytes, such as macrophages and immature dendritic cells, or by local nonprofessional phagocytes, such as epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts (Lauber et al., 2004).
evidence: This represents the prevailing scientific view supported by citation.

claim: Apoptotic cells are infrequently observed in normal human samples due to efficient removal by phagocytes.
source: Although the morphology of apoptotic cells is easily distinguished in histological sections (Kerr et al., 1972), these cells are infrequently observed in normal human samples due to efficient removal by phagocytes (Lauber et al., 2004; Poon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The phagocytes responsible for the removal of apoptotic cells in the homeostatic state remain uncertain.
source: Hence, the phagocytes responsible for the removal of apoptotic cells in the homeostatic state remain uncertain and it is unknown whether they are tissue specific.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Neutrophils represent 50-70% of the total white blood cell population in humans.
source: Neutrophils, a type of terminally differentiated and short-living phagocytic cell, represent 50–70% of the total white blood cell population in humans (Amulic et al., 2012; Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neutrophils are not considered key players in apoptotic cell clearance.
source: However, neutrophils are not considered key players in apoptotic cell clearance (Nagata et al., 2010; Poon et al., 2014).
evidence: This represents the prevailing scientific view prior to the current study, supported by citations.

claim: Neutrophils function as inflammatory cells responsible for killing bacteria and fighting infection.
source: They instead function as inflammatory cells responsible for killing bacteria and fighting infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neutrophil function.

claim: Blood neutrophils swarm to the site of infection where they release toxic mediators that kill microorganisms but can also damage tissues.
source: Blood neutrophils often swarm to the site of infection, where they release toxic mediators (e.g. reactive oxygen species and proteases) that not only kill microorganisms but also can damage tissues (Amulic et al., 2012; Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neutrophil function supported by citations.

claim: Apoptotic cells release 'keep-out' signals such as lactoferrin that prevent the recruitment of neutrophils to the apoptotic site.
source: To prevent inflammation, apoptotic cells have been shown to release 'keep-out' signals, such as lactoferrin, that prevent the recruitment of neutrophils to the apoptotic site (Bournazou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Neutrophils are related to multiple autoimmune diseases.
source: Nevertheless, neutrophils are related to multiple autoimmune diseases (Amulic et al., 2012; Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mild neutropenia was observed to precede and accompany the onset of type 1 diabetes.
source: For example, mild neutropenia was observed to precede and accompany the onset of type 1 diabetes, a typical autoimmune disease (Harsunen et al., 2013; Valle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A large number of neutrophils were observed in hepatocytes in human noncancerous liver tissue obtained from patients with hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: We observed a large number of neutrophils in hepatocytes in human noncancerous liver tissue obtained from patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study supported by microscopy images in Figure 1A.

claim: A large number of neutrophils were observed in hepatocytes in human liver tissue from patients with hepatic hemangioma.
source: We observed a large number of neutrophils in hepatocytes in human noncancerous liver tissue obtained from patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (Figure 1A) or from patients with hepatic hemangioma (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B.

claim: The hepatocytes occupied by neutrophils were apoptotic, as evidenced by condensed chromatin signature.
source: We discovered that the hepatocytes occupied by neutrophils were apoptotic, as evidenced by the condensed chromatin signature (Figure 1A, panels i–vi, black arrowheads indicate condensed chromatin, white arrowheads point to neutrophils with a characteristic multilobed nucleus).
evidence: This is a direct observation supported by microscopy images showing condensed chromatin in Figure 1A.

claim: Apoptotic hepatocytes are rarely observed in the human liver, possibly due to the rapid removal of apoptotic cells by phagocytes.
source: Importantly, apoptotic hepatocytes are rarely observed in the human liver, possibly due to the rapid removal of apoptotic cells by phagocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that apoptotic cells are infrequently seen in normal tissue.

claim: In a total of 281 apoptotic hepatocytes from 32 livers, each apoptotic hepatocyte was engorged by up to 22 neutrophils.
source: In a total of 281 apoptotic hepatocytes from 32 livers, we observed that each apoptotic hepatocyte was engorged by up to 22 neutrophils (Figure 1C, Table 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study presented in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: Apoptotic hepatocytes were confirmed by TUNEL staining or Caspase-3 immunostaining.
source: We also confirmed apoptotic hepatocytes by TUNEL staining or Caspase-3 immunostaining (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is experimental data showing apoptosis confirmation methods presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Neutrophils burrowed inside apoptotic hepatocytes were stained with an antibody against neutrophil elastase, myeloperoxidase, or recognized by their multilobed nucleus signature.
source: Neutrophils burrowed inside apoptotic hepatocytes were either stained with an antibody against neutrophil elastase (NE), myeloperoxidase, or recognized by their multilobed nucleus signature (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the methods used to identify neutrophils, supported by images in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Other immune cells were rarely associated with apoptotic hepatocytes.
source: Other immune cells were rarely associated with apoptotic hepatocytes.
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by immunostaining data.

claim: Kupffer cells are liver-resident phagocytes that are thought to clear apoptotic bodies.
source: Kupffer cells are liver-resident phagocytes that are thought to clear apoptotic bodies (Canbay et al., 2003; Eipel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Few Kupffer cells were observed invading or engulfing apoptotic hepatocytes.
source: Upon staining with an antibody against CD68, a marker of Kupffer cells, we observed few Kupffer cells invading or engulfing apoptotic hepatocytes (Figure 1C,E, 7A and Table 3).
evidence: This is experimental data from immunostaining presented in Figures 1C, 1E, 7A and Table 3.

claim: Few CD11b+ or CD45RA+ cells were detected associated with apoptotic sites.
source: Furthermore, we detected few CD11b+ or CD45RA+ cells associated with the apoptotic sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Tables 4 and 5).
evidence: This is experimental data from immunostaining presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Tables 4 and 5.

claim: Neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic cells consists of three sequential steps: invading/burrowing, phagocytosis/detachment, and complete digestion.
source: Based on the above observations that neutrophils are the predominant phagocyte associated with apoptotic hepatocytes, we hypothesized that the neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic cells consists of the following three sequential steps.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations from microscopy images showing sequential stages of the process.

claim: An average of seven neutrophils enter each apoptotic hepatocyte.
source: We observed an average of seven neutrophils entering each apoptotic hepatocyte, and we termed this process perforocytosis (from Latin perfero to bore) (Figure 1A, white arrowheads point to neutrophils).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Neutrophils within hepatocytes clear apoptotic bodies from the inside without destroying the cellular membrane or extruding the cytoplasm.
source: The neutrophils within hepatocytes appeared to clear apoptotic bodies from the inside without destroying the cellular membrane or extruding the cytoplasm (two burrowed neutrophils phagocytosed apoptotic debris as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy images presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Following digestion by neutrophils, apoptotic hepatocytes decrease in size and detach from nearby hepatocytes.
source: Following digestion by neutrophils, the apoptotic hepatocytes decreased in size, and detached from nearby hepatocytes (Figure 1A, panels iv–vi).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy images presented in Figure 1A.

claim: After clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes, neutrophils migrate away from the cleared space, possibly to make room for new hepatocytes generated by rapid division.
source: After the clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes, neutrophils seemed to migrate away from the cleared space, possibly to make room for new hepatocytes generated by rapid division.
evidence: This is an observation with speculative reasoning about the purpose of neutrophil migration.

claim: The 'eating inside' phagocytosis process differs sharply from the well-known engulfment of apoptotic cells or fragmented apoptotic bodies by macrophages.
source: This 'eating inside' phagocytosis process differed sharply from the well-known engulfment of apoptotic cells or fragmented apoptotic bodies by other phagocytic cells, such as macrophages (Poon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison based on observations in the current study and established knowledge about macrophage phagocytosis.

claim: Neutrophils within apoptotic hepatocytes were confirmed in mouse livers by intravital microscopy and electron microscopy.
source: Neutrophils within apoptotic hepatocytes were confirmed in mouse livers by intravital microscopy (Figure 2A and B) and electron microscopy (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from microscopy presented in Figures 2A, 2B, and 2C.

claim: Apoptotic hepatocytes in wild-type mouse livers were occupied by neutrophils but not associated with macrophages.
source: Similar to the observations in human samples, apoptotic hepatocytes in wild-type (WT) mouse livers were occupied by neutrophils but not associated with macrophages (Figure 2A, neutrophils were labeled with an i.v. injection of anti-Ly6G antibody, macrophages were labeled with anti-F4/80 antibody and apoptotic cells were labeled with Annexin V).
evidence: This is experimental data from intravital microscopy presented in Figure 2A.

claim: A total of 24 apoptotic cells were observed in eight WT livers with an average of two burrowed neutrophils in each mouse apoptotic hepatocyte.
source: A total of 24 apoptotic cells were observed in eight WT livers with an average of two burrowed neutrophils in each mouse apoptotic hepatocyte.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study.

claim: The entire process of neutrophil perforocytosis in mouse livers was visualized using the Cellvizio System.
source: By using the Cellvizio System (Confocal Miniprobes), we managed to visualize the entire process of neutrophil perforocytosis in mouse livers (Figure 2B and Videos 1 and 2, apoptotic hepatocytes were labeled with Annexin V and neutrophils were labeled with anti-Ly6G antibody).
evidence: This is experimental data from intravital microscopy presented in Figure 2B and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Annexin V positive apoptotic hepatocytes were burrowed and cleared by Ly6G-labeled neutrophils.
source: Consistent with observations in human samples, Annexin V positive apoptotic hepatocytes were burrowed and cleared by Ly6G-labeled neutrophils (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data from intravital microscopy presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Neutrophils are able to completely digest apoptotic hepatocytes around 4-7 minutes.
source: This eating inside phagocytic process is fast and rigorous in which neutrophils were able to completely digest apoptotic hepatocytes around 4–7 min (Figure 2B and Videos 1, 2, a total of 13 apoptotic hepatocytes in 12 WT mouse livers were observed).
evidence: This is quantitative data from time-lapse microscopy presented in Figure 2B and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: At the end of the apoptotic clearance process, neutrophils leave the apoptotic sites and are not labeled by Annexin V, indicating neutrophils were not apoptotic.
source: At the end of the apoptotic clearance process, neutrophils simply left the apoptotic sites and were not labeled by Annexin V, indicating neutrophils were not apoptotic.
evidence: This is an observation from intravital microscopy with inference about neutrophil viability.

claim: Human blood neutrophils are able to penetrate and burrow inside human apoptotic hepatocytes induced by puromycin.
source: Human blood neutrophils (labeled with a red membrane dye, PKH-26) were able to penetrate and burrow inside the human apoptotic hepatocytes induced by puromycin (Figure 3B, white arrowheads point to burrowing neutrophils).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro phagocytosis assays presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Apoptotic hepatocytes had markedly decreased size after neutrophil burrowing compared with cells without neutrophil burrowing.
source: These apoptotic hepatocytes had markedly decrease in size after neutrophil burrowing as compared with cells without neutrophil burrowing (Figure 3C and D, Video 3 shows a human neutrophil first burrowed and then started to phagocytose an apoptotic hepatocyte from inside in real time).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro phagocytosis assays presented in Figures 3C, 3D, and Video 3.

claim: Green-labeled HL60 cells showed little response to normal NCTC cells.
source: Green-labeled HL60 cells showed little response to normal NCTC cells (Figure 3E, top row).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro phagocytosis assays presented in Figure 3E.

claim: In the presence of apoptotic NCTC cells, green-labeled HL60 cells polarized and penetrated dead cells.
source: In the presence of apoptotic NCTC cells, however, green-labeled HL60 cells polarized and penetrated dead cells (Figure 3E, white arrowheads point to burrowing neutrophils, bottom row).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro phagocytosis assays presented in Figure 3E.

claim: The phagocytosis of apoptotic hepatocytes by neutrophils was markedly greater than that of normal nonapoptotic hepatocytes.
source: The phagocytosis of apoptotic hepatocytes by neutrophils was markedly greater than that of normal nonapoptotic hepatocytes (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is quantitative data from flow cytometry-based phagocytosis assays presented in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: There was little cytoplasm or DNA leakage during neutrophils phagocytosing apoptotic NCTC cells.
source: There was little cytoplasm or DNA leakage during neutrophils phagocytosing apoptotic NCTC cells as assessed by the extracellular levels of DNA, SOD, and ROS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is experimental data from biochemical assays presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Neutrophils did not phagocytose apoptotic endothelial HUVECs or epithelial HEK293 cells compared with their nonapoptotic controls.
source: To address whether neutrophils also phagocytose other apoptotic cells, we determined the ability of neutrophils to phagocytose apoptotic endothelial HUVECs or epithelial HEK293 cells. We did not observe phagocytosis of these cells compared with their nonapoptotic controls (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is experimental data from phagocytosis assays presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Neutrophils show selectivity in phagocytosing apoptotic hepatocytes.
source: We did not observe phagocytosis of these cells compared with their nonapoptotic controls (Figure 3G), indicating the selectivity of neutrophils in phagocytosing apoptotic hepatocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing differential phagocytosis of different cell types.

claim: U937 cells exhibited much lower phagocytosis of apoptotic NCTC cells than did HL60 cells.
source: Upon comparing the ability of HL60 cells and macrophage U937 cells to phagocytose apoptotic hepatocytes, we found that U937 cells exhibited much lower phagocytosis of apoptotic NCTC cells than did HL60 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from comparative phagocytosis assays presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Similar results were observed with human and mouse macrophages showing lower phagocytosis than neutrophils.
source: Similar results were observed with human and mouse macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C), consistent with the central role of neutrophils in mediating apoptotic hepatocyte clearance.
evidence: This is experimental data from comparative phagocytosis assays presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Apoptotic NCTC cells showed markedly increased secretion of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-12 compared with nonapoptotic controls.
source: Apoptotic NCTC cells showed markedly increased secretion of the cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-12 compared with nonapoptotic controls (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is experimental data from cytokine screening assays presented in Figures 4A–D.

claim: GM-CSF, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, and IL-10 were not significantly changed in apoptotic NCTC cells.
source: In contrast, GM-CSF, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, and IL-10 were not significantly changed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from cytokine screening assays presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of the IL-1β receptor abolished the phagocytosis of apoptotic NCTC cells.
source: Knockdown of the IL-1β receptor abolished the phagocytosis of apoptotic NCTC cells (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is experimental data from receptor knockdown experiments presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Knockdown of the IL-8 receptor showed a 50% reduction in phagocytosis.
source: whereas knockdown of the IL-8 receptor showed a 50% reduction in phagocytosis (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is experimental data from receptor knockdown experiments presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Neutrophil chemoattractants IL-1β and IL-8 secreted by apoptotic NCTC cells are key signals for attracting neutrophils and inducing subsequent phagocytosis.
source: Thus, neutrophil chemoattractants, IL-1β and IL-8, secreted by apoptotic NCTC cells are key signals for attracting neutrophils and inducing subsequent phagocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the receptor knockdown experiments showing abolished or reduced phagocytosis.

claim: Endogenous IL-1β was found associated with apoptotic hepatocytes but not with normal hepatocytes in human liver samples.
source: Consistent with above observations, we found endogenous IL-1β associated with apoptotic hepatocytes but not with normal hepatocytes in human liver samples (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is experimental data from immunostaining of human liver samples presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Apoptotic NCTC cells had markedly increased P-selectin, E-selectin, L-selectin, and PECAM compared with nonapoptotic controls.
source: Next, we examined the cell surface molecules in hepatocytes and found that apoptotic NCTC cells had markedly increased P-selectin, E-selection, L-selectin, and PECAM as compared with nonapoptotic controls (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is experimental data from cell surface molecule analysis presented in Figure 4G.

claim: Inhibition of selectins with a pan-selectin antagonist abrogated the neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes.
source: Inhibition of selectins (with a pan-selectin antagonist, bimosiamose) but not PECAM (with a function blocking antibody) abrogated the neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is experimental data from inhibition experiments presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Selectins play a critical role during neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes.
source: Inhibition of selectins (with a pan-selectin antagonist, bimosiamose) but not PECAM (with a function blocking antibody) abrogated the neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes (Figure 4E), indicating selectins play a critical role during this process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selectin inhibition experiments.

claim: Antibody or genetic depletion yielded about 90% or 70% reduction in mouse peripheral blood neutrophils, respectively.
source: Antibody or genetic depletion yielded about 90% or 70% reduction in mouse peripheral blood neutrophils, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is experimental data from neutrophil depletion experiments presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: After neutrophil depletion, apoptotic bodies were no longer associated with neutrophils.
source: After neutrophil depletion, the apoptotic bodies were no longer associated with neutrophils (Figures 2A, 5A and B).
evidence: This is experimental data from microscopy of neutrophil-depleted mice presented in Figures 2A, 5A and B.

claim: Macrophages were associated with apoptotic hepatocytes in neutrophil-depleted samples.
source: However, we observed that macrophages were associated with apoptotic hepatocytes in neutrophil-depleted samples (Figures 2A, 5A and C), suggesting a compensatory role of macrophages in phagocytosing dead hepatocytes in the absence of neutrophils.
evidence: This is experimental data from microscopy of neutrophil-depleted mice presented in Figures 2A, 5A and C.

claim: Macrophages have a compensatory role in phagocytosing dead hepatocytes in the absence of neutrophils.
source: However, we observed that macrophages were associated with apoptotic hepatocytes in neutrophil-depleted samples (Figures 2A, 5A and C), suggesting a compensatory role of macrophages in phagocytosing dead hepatocytes in the absence of neutrophils.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that macrophages associate with apoptotic hepatocytes after neutrophil depletion.

claim: The percentage of apoptotic hepatocytes in neutrophil-depleted samples was significantly increased compared to controls (0.92% vs 0.2%, p<0.001).
source: The percentage of apoptotic hepatocytes in neutrophil-depleted samples was significantly increased compared to that in controls (0.92% vs 0.2%, p<0.001, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from analysis of neutrophil-depleted mice presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Neutrophil depletion impaired the prompt clearance of apoptotic cells in the mouse liver.
source: Hence, neutrophil depletion impaired the prompt clearance of apoptotic cells in the mouse liver.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased percentage of apoptotic hepatocytes in neutrophil-depleted mice.

claim: Similar results were obtained in neutrophil-depleted mice with or without antibiotic treatment.
source: To rule out the effects of environmental microbes after neutrophil depletion, we also treated the neutrophil-depleted mice with antibiotic (20 mg/kg ampicillin, i.p. injected daily). We obtained similar results in neutrophil-depleted mice with or without antibiotic treatment (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is experimental data from antibiotic treatment experiments presented in Figures 5A–D.

claim: Impaired liver function was observed in neutrophil-depleted livers with increased aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase activity and increased total or direct bilirubin level compared with nontreated controls.
source: Meanwhile, we observed impaired liver function in neutrophil-depleted livers (with increased aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase activity and increased total or direct bilirubin level) compared with nontreated controls (Figure 6A–D, antibody depletion).
evidence: This is experimental data from liver function assays presented in Figures 6A–D.

claim: Depletion of neutrophils had little effect on other tissues such as kidney.
source: Depletion of neutrophils had little effect on other tissues (e.g. kidney, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is experimental data from analysis of other tissues presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: An increase in autoantibodies (against antinuclear antigen, smooth muscle actin, liver-kidney microsome, and total IgG antibodies) was detected in neutrophil-depleted mice compared with controls.
source: In the present study, we detected an increase in autoantibodies (i.e. against antinuclear antigen, smooth muscle actin, liver-kidney microsome, and total IgG antibodies) in neutrophil-depleted mice compared with controls (Figure 6E–H, antibody depletion).
evidence: This is experimental data from autoantibody assays presented in Figures 6E–H.

claim: The increase in autoantibodies was not affected by the treatment of antibiotic.
source: This increase was not affected by the treatment of antibiotic and was not observed in macrophage-depleted mice (Figure 6E–H, macrophages were depleted with clodronate-liposome, see Methods).
evidence: This is experimental data from antibiotic treatment experiments presented in Figures 6E–H.

claim: The increase in autoantibodies was not observed in macrophage-depleted mice.
source: This increase was not affected by the treatment of antibiotic and was not observed in macrophage-depleted mice (Figure 6E–H, macrophages were depleted with clodronate-liposome, see Methods).
evidence: This is experimental data from macrophage depletion experiments presented in Figures 6E–H.

claim: Neutrophil depletion not only impaired apoptotic hepatocyte clearance but also led to the generation of autoantibodies, suggesting a role of defective neutrophil-mediated removal of apoptotic bodies in AIL disease.
source: Hence, neutrophil depletion not only impaired apoptotic hepatocyte clearance but also led to the generation of autoantibodies, suggesting a role of defective neutrophil-mediated removal of apoptotic bodies in AIL disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined observations of impaired clearance and autoantibody generation.

claim: A total of 22 AIL disease patient samples contained apoptotic hepatocytes that were not phagocytosed or invaded by neutrophils.
source: In contrast to the normal human controls, a total of 22 AIL disease patient samples contained apoptotic hepatocytes that were not phagocytosed or invaded by neutrophils (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is experimental data from analysis of AIL patient samples presented in Figure 7A.

claim: More apoptotic bodies were associated with macrophages in AIL disease patient samples, as observed in neutrophil-depleted mouse livers.
source: More apoptotic bodies were associated with macrophages, as observed in neutrophil-depleted mouse livers (Figure 7A, Table 7).
evidence: This is experimental data from analysis of AIL patient samples presented in Figure 7A and Table 7.

claim: The blood neutrophil count in AIL disease patients is within the normal range.
source: Since the blood neutrophil count in AIL disease patients is within the normal range, we surmised potential defects in the phagocytosis ability of neutrophils from AIL disease patients.
evidence: This is an observation from clinical data with inference about potential defects.

claim: Markedly decreased phagocytosis of apoptotic NCTC cells was observed by neutrophils from AIL disease patients compared to normal controls.
source: We observed markedly decreased phagocytosis of apoptotic NCTC cells by neutrophils from AIL disease patients compared to normal controls (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro phagocytosis assays with AIL patient neutrophils presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Normal human neutrophils burrowed into apoptotic NCTC cells and demonstrated perforocytosis, while AIL disease neutrophils exhibited little response toward apoptotic NCTC cells.
source: Normal human neutrophils burrowed into apoptotic NCTC cells and demonstrated perforocytosis, while AIL disease neutrophils exhibited little response toward apoptotic NCTC cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro phagocytosis assays presented in Figure 7C.

claim: The expression of IL-1β receptor IL1R1 and selectin binding protein P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL-1) was markedly decreased in AIL neutrophils compared with normal human neutrophils.
source: We noted that the expression of IL-1β receptor, IL1R1 and selectin binding protein, P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL-1) was markedly decreased in AIL neutrophils as compared with normal human neutrophils (Figure 7D)
evidence: This is experimental data from microarray analysis presented in Figure 7D.

claim: The decreased expression of IL1R1 and PSGL-1 in AIL neutrophils further confirmed the critical roles of IL-1β and selectins in neutrophil-mediated apoptotic clearance.
source: We noted that the expression of IL-1β receptor, IL1R1 and selectin binding protein, P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL-1) was markedly decreased in AIL neutrophils as compared with normal human neutrophils (Figure 7D), which further confirmed the critical roles of IL-1β and selectins in neutrophil-mediated apoptotic clearance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between decreased receptor expression and impaired phagocytosis in AIL neutrophils.

claim: The finding of neutrophil burrowing into and clearing of apoptotic hepatocytes under physiological conditions reveals a fundamental mechanism for the removal of effete hepatocytes.
source: Our finding of neutrophil burrowing into and clearing of apoptotic hepatocytes under physiological conditions reveals a fundamental mechanism for the removal of effete hepatocytes
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Professional phagocytes have much higher phagocytic efficiency and capacity than nonprofessional phagocytes, but they are greatly outnumbered by other cell types in tissues.
source: In general, professional phagocytes have much higher phagocytic efficiency and capacity than nonprofessional phagocytes, but they are greatly outnumbered by other cell types in tissues (Elliott and Ravichandran, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Monocytes make up less than 10% of the total white blood cell population.
source: Compared to macrophages or their precursors, monocytes, which make up less than 10% of the total white blood cell population, neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells (up to 70%) in humans
evidence: This is established knowledge about blood cell composition.

claim: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells (up to 70%) in humans.
source: Compared to macrophages or their precursors, monocytes, which make up less than 10% of the total white blood cell population, neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells (up to 70%) in humans
evidence: This is established knowledge about blood cell composition.

claim: Neutrophils are ideally suited for the swift clearance of apoptotic hepatic cells due to their abundance.
source: Compared to macrophages or their precursors, monocytes, which make up less than 10% of the total white blood cell population, neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells (up to 70%) in humans, and thus ideally suited for the swift clearance of apoptotic hepatic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high abundance of neutrophils and their observed phagocytic function.

claim: Macrophages were induced to phagocytose apoptotic hepatocytes following the depletion of circulating neutrophils.
source: As macrophages were induced to phagocytose apoptotic hepatocytes following the depletion of circulating neutrophils, our data show compensatory activation of other phagocytes under these conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from neutrophil depletion experiments.

claim: The data show compensatory activation of other phagocytes under neutrophil depletion conditions.
source: As macrophages were induced to phagocytose apoptotic hepatocytes following the depletion of circulating neutrophils, our data show compensatory activation of other phagocytes under these conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that macrophages associate with apoptotic hepatocytes after neutrophil depletion.

claim: Neutrophils do not phagocytose apoptotic epithelial and endothelial cells.
source: As neutrophils do not phagocytose apoptotic epithelial and endothelial cells, it is possible that distinct signals are specifically released by different types of apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro phagocytosis assays.

claim: It is possible that distinct signals are specifically released by different types of apoptotic cells.
